title: AP African American Studies
summary: Connect African societies, resistance, freedom and modern movements through careful source analysis.
frameworkNote: 2026–27 structure checked against College Board on 15 October 2026: 4 units. Original VertexED focused lessons and self-check questions sample each unit; they do not replace the full course framework, required materials or teacher review. The course also includes an individual student project; these exercises are preparation, not a submitted or assessed project.

modules.title: African societies and connected worlds
modules.focus: Use regional evidence to challenge a single-story account of Africa.
explanation: Africa contained diverse political systems, languages and trading networks before Atlantic slavery. Mali’s trans-Saharan connections and the Swahili coast’s Indian Ocean connections show different routes through which goods, beliefs and knowledge travelled.
A source reveals a particular viewpoint. Read an artefact alongside its place, date and purpose; a traveller’s description alone cannot represent every resident or an entire continent.

workedExample.prompt: Compare a map of Mali’s trade routes with one of Swahili coastal ports.
steps: Identify Mali’s links across the Sahara and the ports’ maritime connections.
Explain that both supported exchange, while their geography and trading partners differed.

misconception.claim: African history begins with Atlantic enslavement.
misconception.correction: Complex African societies and global connections preceded that trade by centuries.

questions.prompt: Why would a single European travel account be insufficient evidence of life in medieval Mali?
questions.answer: It reflects one visitor’s access and assumptions; local material, oral and written evidence can reveal other experiences.
checkpoints: Identify perspective
Explain a corroborating source

questions.prompt: How could imported pottery at an East African port support an argument about exchange?
questions.answer: Its origin can support contact through trade, but it does not alone prove how all residents lived.
checkpoints: Connect object to exchange
Limit the inference

questions.prompt: Why is describing Africa before Atlantic slavery only as a source of enslaved labour historically inadequate?
questions.answer: It projects a later system backwards. It omits varied states, communities and exchange networks. African societies should be studied through their own institutions and historical changes.
checkpoints: It projects a later system backwards.
It omits varied states, communities and exchange networks.
African societies should be studied through their own institutions and historical changes.

questions.prompt: A foreign traveller describes one African court as wealthy. What can and cannot be inferred?
questions.answer: The account offers evidence about that court as the traveller represented it. Its purpose and access shape the description. It does not establish that every household or society had the same wealth.
checkpoints: The account offers evidence about that court as the traveller represented it.
Its purpose and access shape the description.
It does not establish that every household or society had the same wealth.

notes.title: African societies and connected worlds in depth
paragraphs: Comparing Mali and Swahili coastal communities reveals different forms of African connection before the Atlantic slave trade. Mali participated in trans-Saharan networks linking gold-producing regions with northern markets, while Swahili ports connected eastern Africa to Indian Ocean exchange. Transport, political authority and urban institutions shaped who benefited. Islam circulated through these networks but did not erase local languages or practices. A trade map shows possible connections, not the complete experience of every resident. Combine it with archaeological evidence and carefully situated accounts to explain exchange without reducing societies to commodities alone.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare a hypothetical caravan town taxing gold traffic with a coastal port servicing seasonal shipping.
steps: Both obtain resources from exchange, but their routes and transport constraints differ.
Caravan protection and water access matter inland; harbour facilities and sailing seasons matter at the coast.
workedExamples.conclusion: A shared commercial role can coexist with distinct institutions and environments.

flashcards.front: What connected Mali to northern markets?
What connected Swahili ports to distant regions?
Does religious diffusion erase local practices automatically?
What can a trade map not show alone?
flashcards.back: Every resident's experience or the full distribution of benefits.

diagrams.title: Two routes of exchange
diagrams.description: The comparison identifies a shared function and different mechanisms.

nodes.label: Caravan town
nodes.detail: Overland movement depends on routes and water.

nodes.label: Coastal port
nodes.detail: Maritime movement depends on harbours and sailing conditions.

nodes.label: Commercial centres
nodes.detail: Both can link local production to distant demand.

modules.title: Enslavement, community and resistance
modules.focus: Distinguish a system of coercion from the choices people made within it.
explanation: Atlantic slavery forcibly displaced Africans and treated people as property under changing colonial laws. Enslaved people nevertheless sustained relationships, adapted cultural practices and resisted through escape, work slowdowns, legal claims and revolt.

Resistance differed by circumstance and risk. When reading a freedom narrative, examine the writer’s purpose and audience while taking testimony seriously; compare it with other evidence rather than assuming either perfect neutrality or worthlessness.

workedExample.prompt: Explain why escape and preserving family ties can both be studied as resistance.
steps: Escape directly challenged an enslaver’s control over movement and labour.
Protecting relationships resisted a system that threatened separation and denied independent family authority.

misconception.claim: Only armed revolt counts as resistance.
misconception.correction: Resistance also included everyday, cultural, legal and collective actions.

questions.prompt: Why does an abolitionist audience matter when analysing a published freedom narrative?
questions.answer: The author may select experiences to challenge slavery and persuade readers; this purpose shapes presentation without automatically invalidating the account.
checkpoints: Identify audience
Connect purpose to presentation

questions.prompt: What extra evidence would strengthen a claim that enslaved communities preserved cultural practices?
questions.answer: Material objects, language, music or multiple testimonies can corroborate patterns across people and places.
checkpoints: Name relevant evidence
Explain corroboration

questions.prompt: Why should a successful escape not be treated as evidence that escape was equally available to everyone?
questions.answer: Routes, contacts and resources varied. Family responsibilities and surveillance affected options. One success cannot represent all people's opportunities or risks.
checkpoints: Routes, contacts and resources varied.
Family responsibilities and surveillance affected options.
One success cannot represent all people's opportunities or risks.

questions.prompt: How can a freedom narrative and a sale record answer different historical questions?
hints: Avoid letting administrative language define the person.
questions.answer: The narrative can describe experience and interpretation. The sale record can document transactions and imposed legal status. Reading them together reveals both institutional coercion and a person's account without treating either as complete.
checkpoints: The narrative can describe experience and interpretation.
The sale record can document transactions and imposed legal status.
Reading them together reveals both institutional coercion and a person's account without treating either as complete.

notes.title: Enslavement, community and resistance in depth
paragraphs: Enslavement depended on organised coercion, not a loss of the humanity or agency of the people enslaved. Law, violence, sale and forced labour constrained choices and threatened families. Resistance therefore took varied forms under unequal risks, including flight, collective revolt, negotiations over work and efforts to sustain relationships. Not every survival action should be labelled resistance without context, but apparently private acts can challenge control over daily life. Freedom narratives combine testimony with an audience and persuasive purpose. Those features call for careful interpretation and corroboration, not automatic dismissal of the speaker's experience.

workedExamples.prompt: Analyse a hypothetical record in which an enslaved parent negotiates time to visit a child sold to another household.
steps: The separation shows the coercive power of sale over family life.
The request seeks to preserve a relationship within severe constraints.
workedExamples.conclusion: It can show agency and a challenge to imposed separation without suggesting that negotiation made the system voluntary.

flashcards.back: A system treating enslaved people as property under law.

flashcards.front: Does agency mean freedom from coercion?

flashcards.back: Risks, resources and aims differed by circumstance.

flashcards.front: Does a persuasive purpose invalidate testimony?
flashcards.back: No; analyse its evidence and context.

diagrams.title: Family under coercion
diagrams.description: The relationship persists within imposed constraints.

nodes.label: Preserved relationship
nodes.detail: Agency challenges one effect of control.

modules.title: Freedom after emancipation
modules.focus: Separate constitutional change from access to power and resources.
explanation: The Reconstruction Amendments abolished slavery, established national citizenship and equal protection, and prohibited denying voting rights on grounds of race. Enforcement, political violence and economic dependence shaped how these rights operated in practice.

African Americans built schools, businesses, organisations and artistic movements while resisting exclusion. The Great Migration combined pressures such as racial violence with opportunities elsewhere; migration did not remove discrimination from destination cities.

workedExample.prompt: Explain how a Black school founded after emancipation could express freedom.
steps: Education increased opportunities to read contracts, participate politically and pursue work.
Community control of institutions also asserted collective priorities despite unequal resources.

misconception.claim: A constitutional right guarantees equal practical access.
misconception.correction: Enforcement and social conditions can limit access even when a right exists in law.

questions.prompt: How could a poll tax weaken voting access without explicitly naming race?
questions.hint: Consider unequal resources and historical context.
questions.answer: A payment requirement could exclude poor voters and operate alongside violence and discriminatory administration to suppress Black participation.
checkpoints: Identify mechanism
Explain context

questions.prompt: Give one push and one pull factor in the Great Migration.
questions.hint: Separate departure pressures from destination attractions.
questions.answer: Racial violence pushed people from the South; industrial jobs attracted many to northern and midwestern cities.
checkpoints: Name a push factor
Name a pull factor

questions.prompt: Explain why a Black community's investment in a school after emancipation can be political as well as educational.
questions.answer: The school develops literacy and learning. Collective funding and governance assert community priorities. It can support broader participation and autonomy despite exclusion.
checkpoints: The school develops literacy and learning.
Collective funding and governance assert community priorities.
It can support broader participation and autonomy despite exclusion.

questions.prompt: A migrant finds higher wages but faces housing exclusion. How should the move be evaluated?
questions.answer: Higher wages indicate an economic opportunity. Housing exclusion limits access and security. The experience shows uneven change across dimensions of freedom and well-being.
checkpoints: Higher wages indicate an economic opportunity.
Housing exclusion limits access and security.
The experience shows uneven change across dimensions of freedom and well-being.

notes.title: Freedom after emancipation in depth
paragraphs: The Reconstruction Amendments changed constitutional status but did not make enforcement automatic. The Thirteenth Amendment prohibited slavery and involuntary servitude while retaining an exception for punishment after conviction; the Fourteenth established citizenship rules and protections against state denial of due process and equal protection; the Fifteenth prohibited voting discrimination based on race, colour or previous servitude. Violence and exclusion still restricted practical rights. African Americans built institutions and pursued mobility. The Great Migration moved millions from the South towards northern and western cities, where new opportunities coexisted with discrimination and racial violence.

workedExamples.prompt: Analyse a hypothetical town where Black citizens register to vote but face threats at the polling place.
steps: Registration shows a formal route to participation.
Threats obstruct the exercise of that right even without changing the written constitutional protection.
workedExamples.conclusion: The case distinguishes legal status, enforcement and lived access.

flashcards.front: What did the Thirteenth Amendment retain?
What does equal protection concern in the Fourteenth?
flashcards.back: State treatment of persons under law.

flashcards.front: What discrimination does the Fifteenth prohibit?
flashcards.back: Voting discrimination based on race, colour or previous servitude.

diagrams.title: Rights and effective access
diagrams.description: A legal change needs conditions that permit its exercise.

nodes.label: Practical participation
nodes.detail: People can exercise the protected right.

modules.title: Movements, strategies and research claims
modules.focus: Compare change strategies without treating a movement as a single voice.
explanation: Twentieth-century freedom movements used litigation, boycotts, organising, direct action and cultural expression. Organisations sometimes shared aims while disagreeing over tactics, leadership or the relationship between legal equality and economic justice.

A research argument should define a manageable question and connect specific evidence to a claim. Different forms of evidence answer different questions: a speech reveals an argument, while participation records may illuminate an organisation’s reach.

workedExample.prompt: Compare a legal challenge to segregation with a sustained bus boycott.
steps: The court case sought an enforceable ruling within legal institutions.
The boycott combined economic pressure and collective action; the two strategies could reinforce each other.

misconception.claim: Civil rights organisations all used the same strategy.
misconception.correction: Their priorities, constituencies and methods varied and changed over time.

questions.prompt: What makes “How did local organising sustain one boycott?” more researchable than “How did freedom happen?”
questions.answer: It identifies a bounded event and mechanism that can be investigated with meeting records, testimony and contemporary reporting.
checkpoints: Identify narrower scope
Name usable evidence

questions.prompt: Can a movement’s song alone establish the number of its supporters?
questions.answer: No. It can reveal ideas and cultural expression; participation counts require additional evidence with known coverage.
checkpoints: Limit the claim
Identify suitable evidence

questions.prompt: Turn 'Was the movement successful?' into a bounded research question about a local campaign.
questions.answer: Ask how a named campaign changed access to a specified service during a defined period. Use implementation and participation evidence. Keep wider equality claims outside what that evidence alone can establish.
checkpoints: Ask how a named campaign changed access to a specified service during a defined period.
Use implementation and participation evidence.
Keep wider equality claims outside what that evidence alone can establish.

questions.prompt: Why should a leader's speech not be used alone to estimate a movement's membership?
questions.answer: A speech communicates argument and mobilisation. It does not count all participants reliably. Membership records, attendance evidence and their limitations are more relevant to reach.
checkpoints: A speech communicates argument and mobilisation.
It does not count all participants reliably.
Membership records, attendance evidence and their limitations are more relevant to reach.

notes.title: Movements, strategies and research claims in depth
paragraphs: Freedom movements combined organisational labour with visible public action. A boycott requires communication, alternative transport, fundraising and sustained participation; a court case requires evidence, plaintiffs and legal argument. These strategies can reinforce one another rather than compete as isolated choices. A movement's public speeches reveal aims and persuasion, while meeting minutes or participation records can show how work was coordinated. Distinguish legal desegregation from broader economic equality when judging outcomes. A research question should specify a place, period and mechanism so that success is assessed against evidence rather than assumed from a famous event.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare a hypothetical campaign's court challenge with its organised refusal to use a segregated service.
steps: The legal challenge seeks an enforceable ruling.
The boycott applies economic and public pressure but depends on practical support for participants.
workedExamples.conclusion: The strategies can interact, while their effects need separate evidence.

flashcards.front: What sustains a boycott beyond a speech?
Does desegregation alone establish economic equality?

diagrams.title: Coordinated pressure
diagrams.description: Different strategies can support a common campaign.

nodes.label: Boycott and litigation
nodes.detail: Economic pressure and legal argument act through different mechanisms.

nodes.label: Institutional change
nodes.detail: Outcomes must be assessed through implementation.
